steps.what: Confirm purchases and payment choice with the customer
Enter purchases in cash registers and check the displayed total
Take payment and provide change and the receipt

tasks.design: Configure frequently used item buttons in the {OTHER} point-of-sale till to reduce catalogue searching and repeated modifier entry. The attendant still confirms the purchase, checks the final transaction and handles payment and change.
tasks.previous_blocker: A long item list makes routine entry slower than the payment itself.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing till favourites and item groups may shorten entry without custom software.
tasks.still_hard: Unexpected discounts, cash differences and customer corrections remain human work.
tasks.human_edge: The attendant notices a mismatch between what the customer wants and what the till shows.
tasks.altitude: A little more time is available to help the waiting customer; payment authority does not change.

evidence.claim: Native till favourites can reduce navigation and repeated item entry; the time estimate is unmeasured.

assumptions: Boundary is individual till sales, not closing or cash reconciliation. OTHER means the point-of-sale till.

The attendant produces item code, quantity, modifier and payment choice from the purchase in s1 and enters and checks them in s2, whose retained 28 hours include all capture. Missing catalogue matches use ordinary manual till entry.

Test native favourites before code. The author saves the transaction in the same till without a separate approval stage or claimed save-time reduction. Existing arithmetic and receipt printing earn no new labour saving.
The 1-hour upkeep allowance covers item-button corrections; there is no additional automated send or posting in this design.
unknowns: Actual till search time and native favourites support
research_questions: Do configured buttons reduce entry time without increasing correction rates?

already_counted.description: Purchase confirmation, transaction checking and payment handling

approvals.approved_version: The exact spoken purchase and payment confirmation; changes require a fresh confirmation

steps.what: Inspect clean supplies and judge the immediate replenishment need
Collect adequate linens, silverware, glassware, dishes and trays
Stock service stations and check cleanliness and accessibility

tasks.design: Keep the visual check, collection and placement as physical work. A {DOCS} checklist would only help where an existing written replenishment list is actually used; none is assumed here.
tasks.previous_blocker: The useful information is the physical condition and location of clean items.
tasks.enabler_now: No software change removes the handling described by this task.
tasks.still_hard: Broken or dirty items and a sudden rush require local decisions.
tasks.human_edge: The attendant distinguishes usable stock from items that must return for cleaning.
tasks.altitude: The work and decision rights stay the same.

evidence.claim: Visual checks and manual replenishment are physical work; no clerical record is assumed in this baseline.

assumptions: Boundary includes deciding what to fetch, fetching and placing clean supplies. Purchasing and dishwashing are distinct tasks.
There is no structured par-level input or stock database in this design. The attendant produces the replenishment choice by inspection in s1; its entire 25 hours remain counted.
No routine replenishment record, lookup or send is assumed. If a site keeps a stock sheet, measure that real write separately before making a saving claim.
Native tools would be tested before custom work if a written process exists. Upkeep is zero because nothing is installed or maintained.
unknowns: Whether the site actually keeps a written replenishment sheet
research_questions: Does any current clerical stock activity occur during routine replenishment?

incremental.description: No new system or maintained record

time_saved_range_pct.basis: E1 B100 R100 and0 upkeep, net0. Both bounds retain inspection25, collection35 and placement40; neither a template nor a stock view removes physical work without an actual record baseline.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

steps.what: Clarify the items requested by customers
Locate the requested item and check its suitability
Point out or hand over the item to the customer

tasks.design: Retain request clarification, the physical search and the customer handoff. A {DOCS} location list only merits configuration if staff already consult one; a new inventory map would introduce capture and upkeep rather than remove the handling.
tasks.previous_blocker: Items move between stations and the storeroom during service.
tasks.enabler_now: No supported existing location database is assumed.
tasks.still_hard: An apparently similar item may not meet the customer's need.
tasks.human_edge: The attendant can inspect the actual item and explain a suitable alternative.
tasks.altitude: No change to responsibility or time is established.

reach.role: Hosts and Hostesses, Restaurant, Lounge, and Coffee Shop

evidence.claim: Finding movable service items usually requires local observation; a digital location list is not assumed to exist.

assumptions: Boundary includes understanding, locating and handing over or directing. No request ticket or completion record is routinely kept in this baseline.
The customer supplies the request in s1 and the attendant establishes the location and suitability in s2; all 75 hours remain counted. No machine consumes an unproduced stock or location flag.
A native list would be tested before custom software only if an actual written lookup exists. No template removes the physical search in the present design.
Zero upkeep follows from retaining the current physical process without a new map, logging requirement or system.
unknowns: Whether a current location sheet is consulted for any material share of requests
research_questions: How much search time is caused by a missing location reference rather than physically moving items?
